title: Replace public popularity metrics with trending
description: Why this issue exists: the public install-count popularity surface should not expose proprietary/raw metrics as the main user-facing signal. What needs to be done: design and implement a straightforward TRENDING signal that replaces default popularity/count output where appropriate, update ranking/columns/docs/tests, and keep raw analytics private/internal unless explicitly retained for cache internals.
notes:
Implemented per user's design decisions (asked via clarifying questions):
1. Trending formula built from scratch (not a relabel of the old composite score):
   Package.trending in model.py compares the most recent 30d install rate against
   a span-weighted historical baseline derived from the 90d/365d windows
   (days 30-90 and 90-365 as separate rate buckets), expressed as a signed
   percentage (+72%/-11%), clamped to +/-300%, with confidence shrinkage
   (volume/(volume+K)) so low-volume packages don't read as huge swings.
2. Raw install counts (30d/90d/365d) kept as fully opt-in sort/columns
   (-s 30d, -c 30d, etc.) — nothing removed from the public surface.
3. Default sort changed to "trending"; default columns changed to
   name,trending,auto,description where "auto" (new pseudo-column in columns.py)
   is resolved after ranking to whichever of 30d/90d/365d has data on the
   top-ranked result.

Old ad hoc "popularity" composite score (log-volume + discrete trend multiplier
bands) removed entirely; "pop"/"popularity"/"score"/"rank" kept as backward-compat
column aliases pointing at "trending".

Course-correction during review: initial K=50 shrinkage constant was too weak —
verified against the real seed cache that a "json" search buried jq (89k
installs/mo) at #15 while a 3-install/mo package ranked #7. Presented the actual
before/after output to the user; they chose a much stronger volume floor
(K=2000). Re-verified: jq now ranks #5, micro-volume noise no longer dominates
generic searches.

Also verified against the real bundled seed cache (not just mocks) that 90d/365d
analytics are present so trending isn't degenerate on a fresh install.

Updated: model.py, columns.py (trending column + auto pseudo-column +
pick_representative_metric), config.py defaults, options.py (sort aliases,
rank() metric_key), cli.py (help text, deferred default-column resolution,
random command sort choices). Docs: AGENTS.md CLI contract, docs/cli-design.md,
docs/vision.md, docs/product-spec.md (superseded the old "trend score is not
MVP/undecided" language). Tests: 218->219 passing, ruff clean, verify.py green.
close_reason: Trending signal implemented from scratch (recent-vs-historical-baseline ratio with volume shrinkage), replacing raw install counts as the default ranking/column; raw counts kept opt-in. Tuned shrinkage constant with user against real seed-cache output after catching that the initial value let 3-install packages outrank jq. Ranking/columns/config/docs/tests all updated, 219 tests passing.

title: Recalibrate trending formula: penalize new-to-tracking/recently-accelerated packages
description: Package.trending (brewq-sbe's pseudocount-smoothed multiplier) still let packages new to Homebrew analytics tracking (near-zero installs before their most recent 90d window) read as huge adoption spikes -- e.g. bun ~156-271x on installs that are almost entirely within the last 90 days, sdl2-compat 271x on 1 pre-90d install. brewq-253 worked around this by demoting trending from the default sort, but the TREND column itself (still shown by default, still available via -s trending) remained misleading.
design: Anchor the 'recent' rate on the 90d window (installs_90d/3, a several-week smoothed rate) instead of the raw 30d snapshot -- this naturally dampens bursts concentrated entirely in the last 30 days, whether from a brand-new package or an established one whose rate only picked up recently. Layer a graduated pseudocount boost (alpha scales up to 3x at zero pre-90d installs, tapering linearly to 1x by 1500 pre-90d installs) rather than a hard age cutoff or full Bayesian shrinkage to neutral -- calibrated interactively against live cache data (bun, sdl2-compat, openlogi, gcc@15, beets, github-copilot-app as artifacts; pup, libgccjit, eigen@3, dua-cli, jq, ripgrep, git as genuine/established growth) at alpha=30, boost=2.0, threshold=1500.
acceptance_criteria: Package.trending recalibrated in model.py; test_model.py covers the new formula shape and maturity-damping behavior; docs (AGENTS.md, product-spec.md, vision.md) describe the new formula; full suite + scripts/verify.py green.
close_reason: Recalibrated Package.trending: recent rate anchored on installs_90d/3 (several-week smoothed rate) instead of raw installs_30d, and the pseudocount (now alpha=30) scales up to 3x at zero pre-90d installs, tapering linearly to 1x by 1500 pre-90d installs (_TREND_MATURITY_BOOST/_TREND_MATURITY_THRESHOLD). Calibrated interactively against live cache data: bun 156x->21.5x, sdl2-compat 271x->23.0x, openlogi 100x->8.3x, gcc@15 54x->5.0x while established packages (jq 1.4x, ripgrep 1.8x, git 0.9x, dua-cli 1.0x) stay near their original values. Updated model.py, test_model.py (2 tests updated/added), and AGENTS.md/product-spec.md/vision.md/cli-design.md. 221 tests passing, ruff clean.

title: Default to 90d absolute install counts: sort, standard metric, and column order
description:
bun's ~250x trending multiplier is very likely a new-package artifact (recently
added/tracked in Homebrew analytics, not a real adoption spike), which shows
sorting by a self-relative growth multiplier can surface "new and used a
little" packages ahead of genuinely trustworthy, widely-used ones -- the
opposite of what a default sort should optimize for.

Reverse course from brewq-4it/brewq-sbe: make raw absolute install volume the
default signal again, and standardize on the 90d window instead of 30d (90d is
less noisy than 30d and less stale than 365d). Keep trending as an available,
demoted signal rather than removing it.

Concrete changes:
1. Default sort (-s / config `search.sort`) becomes `90d` (raw installs_90d),
   not `trending`. `-t`/`--top` help text ("top N by trending rank") and any
   sort-default fallbacks in options.py need to follow.

title: Replace ratio+clamp trending with pseudocount-smoothed multiplier
description: Current trending = ratio*confidence clamped to +-300% ties dozens of packages at the ceiling and hides brand-new packages entirely (baseline<=0 -> None). Replace with a Laplace/DESeq2-style pseudocount-smoothed ratio (recent+a)/(baseline+a), displayed as a plain multiplier (e.g. 4.1x) instead of a percent. Removes the hard clamp and the separate ad hoc confidence factor -- pseudocount alone damps low-volume noise while preserving real signal for high-volume and genuinely-new-and-surging packages. Calibrated alpha=20 against live cache data.
acceptance_criteria: model.trending returns a multiplier (1.0=neutral) with no hard clamp; columns display as Nx; all tests updated; docs (cli-design/vision/product-spec/AGENTS) describe multiplier semantics
close_reason: Replaced ratio*confidence+clamp with pseudocount-smoothed multiplier (alpha=20, calibrated against live cache: beets 219x->10.3x, bun stays ~250x as genuine signal, jq/git/ripgrep land 0.8x-1.6x near neutral, gcc@15 brand-new-surge now visible at 54.4x instead of hidden as None). Display changed from signed percent to Nx multiplier. No hard ceiling -- eliminates the tie-cluster-at-+300% bug. Updated model.py, columns.py, tests, and cli-design/vision/product-spec/AGENTS docs. 219 tests passing, ruff clean.

title: Prevent configuration defaults from mutating across loads

acceptance_criteria: A regression test loads with an environment override, removes it, and observes the built-in default on the next load; file overrides also cannot mutate DEFAULTS; existing config behavior remains unchanged.
close_reason: Deep-copied built-in config defaults on each load and added regressions for environment and caller mutation leakage; full suite and Ruff pass.

title: Reject invalid search and list row limits

notes:
Grounded in Chris research on fd/rg/jq/fzf/gh/docker/npm/aws-cli conventions
before editing (per feedback-research-before-editing memory). Key finding:
reference CLIs don't inline "only applies when X" caveats into one-line --help
descriptions -- that nuance belongs in fuller docs. Applied:

   aliases that -s already showed for the same 30d/90d/365d concepts -- now
   both show them, satisfying "make 30d/90d/365d treatment consistent."
3. list subcommand's -c help was a vague "Explicit columns: comma-joined keys"
   with zero enumerated keys, unlike search's -c; replaced with an inlined
   column list matching search's style/format.
4. Filled real gaps: list --limit had NO help text at all; config's `path`
   positional had none either. Both fixed.
5. Unified --tsv wording between search and list (previously two different
   phrasings for the same behavior); replaced list --analytics's
   implementation-leaking "(cache-backed)" wording with accurate
   "Add a 30d install-count column" (verified against

   against docs/cli-design.md:168 which already said "inserts 30d").
6. Verified live: `brewq list -c name,trending,bin --limit 3` against the real
   seed cache renders trending percentages and binaries correctly.

Deliberately did NOT add new aliases beyond trend/hot (added in brewq-4it).
Chris's research found no reference tool listing 3+ synonyms per concept in
--help; brewq's existing aliases (n/t/v/d/i/h, one per concept) already match
that restraint. If the intent behind "add more intuitive aliases" was for
something specific beyond trend/hot, that's still open -- flagging rather than
guessing at more.

title: brewq: visual themes, margins, color schemes
description: Config-driven terminal appearance: themes (dark/light/custom), column spacing, margin sizes, color palette for formula/cask/status. Possibly NO_COLOR/ANSI_THEME env var support.

title: brewq: 10x speed — cache binary format + lazy JSON
description: Current ~1s startup is Python overhead loading 16k packages from JSON each run. Needs: msgpack/pickle binary cache, lazy loading with index, or precompiled lookup. Goal: <100ms.
notes: Stabilization baseline 793c774 already includes pickle loading and slotted records. This issue remains open: benchmark the complete cache.load plus inventory/render path before more storage changes. The old load_packages microbenchmark excludes inventory overlay; the 10x goal is not evidence of achieved performance.

title: Add cache-backed autocomplete suggestions for brew and brewq
description:
Add an autocomplete/suggestion surface that uses the maintained brewq cache as the package-name source instead of shelling out repeatedly.

Scope:
- Suggest formula and cask names from the local cache for brewq commands.
- Explore whether and how the same cache can back suggestions for brew command arguments without turning brewq into a brew manager.
- Keep behavior read-only and aligned with brewq query + analytics framing.
- Make cache freshness/fallback behavior visible if suggestions depend on stale or missing cache data.

Open decisions:
- Which shells are first-class for the initial release.
- Whether brew integration is a generated completion file, an opt-in shell widget, or deferred after brewq-only completion.
- Whether suggestions include analytics metadata or only names.

comments.author: Ivan Cherniukh
comments.text:
Plan for later pickup:

Recommended first slice is zsh-only brewq completion, not broad brew integration. Add a generated completion script via `brewq completion zsh`, backed by a hidden/internal package-name completion command that reads `cache.load_packages()` and prints raw cached names only. Static completion should cover brewq commands/options/subcommands; dynamic query suggestions should use cache only, perform no refresh/network work, and return no package suggestions when cache is missing. Suggest names only, not analytics metadata. Defer bash/fish support and brew command integration until brewq completion itself proves useful.

Reasoning: keeps the public interface small, avoids shell scripts parsing cache JSON directly, and avoids turning brewq into brew wrapper/dotfile plumbing before the main query/list experience is fast and polished.

title: brewq: extended package metadata (cross-PM, security, tags)
description: Phase 2 enrichment: cross-check with MacPorts/pip/npm; community engagement (GitHub stars/issues); 3rd-party security scan status; configurability level; tags/categories. Requires additional data sources and likely a separate enrichment cache.

title: Investigate package last-updated metadata column
description: Deferred — tap git-history is not available in brew info --json=v2 (generated_date is site-wide, not per-package). GitHub commits API exists but needs authentication and would require hundreds of hours to backfill all formulae. Installed-time is in the cache but is a different column (local install age vs maintainer activity). Revisit when cache enrichment strategy adds git-based metadata.
